title: Pipes and Cisterns
tagline: Year 2 — Inlet pipes, outlet pipes and leaks as positive and negative work rates

introduction.overview: Pipes and cisterns is time and work with water. An inlet pipe fills a tank (positive rate) and an outlet pipe or leak empties it (negative rate). A pipe that fills a tank in n hours does 1/n of the tank per hour. When several pipes work together, add their rates, with a minus sign for outlets.
introduction.placementRelevance: Pipes and cisterns questions are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds. They look different from time-and-work but use the same method.
introduction.realWorldContext: Filling and draining swimming pools, water tanks with leaks and reservoirs with inlets and outlets are real examples.

learningObjectives: Convert fill and empty times into rates
Handle a leak that makes the filling time longer
Solve problems where pipes are opened and closed at different times
Compute the time to fill or empty a given fraction of the tank

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Rate of an inlet = 1/time to fill. Rate of an outlet = −1/time to empty. Net rate = sum of rates.

coreDefinitions: Inlet: a pipe that fills the tank. Outlet: a pipe that empties it.
Leak: an unintended outlet at the bottom.
Net rate: sum of inlet rates minus outlet rates.
Cistern: a tank or reservoir holding water.
Capacity: the volume of the tank (total work = 1).
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: A tank is a job; an inlet works towards it and an outlet works against it. If the net rate is positive the tank fills, and if negative it empties. The time to complete is 1 divided by the size of the net rate.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Take the capacity as the LCM of all the times. Then each pipe does a whole number of litres per hour and the net rate is simple arithmetic.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Rate
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: n is the time to fill or empty alone.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Time together
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Fills or empties the whole tank.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Leak
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: The pipe alone vs with leak.

mainNarrative: Write each pipe as a rate. A pipe that fills the tank in 10 hours is +1/10 per hour. An outlet that empties in 15 hours is −1/15. With both open the net rate is 1/10 − 1/15 = 1/30 per hour, and the tank is filled in 30 hours.
Use the LCM trick. For fill times 6, 8 and an empty time 12, take capacity 24 litres. Rates are +4, +3 and −2, net +5, so the tank fills in 24 ÷ 5 = 4.8 hours.
A leak makes filling take longer. If a pipe fills the tank in 6 hours but it takes 7.5 hours with the leak, the leak rate is 1/6 − 1/7.5 = 1/30, so the leak alone empties a full tank in 30 hours.
If pipes are opened for different durations, add the work done by each. Pipe A (12 hours) open for 4 hours fills 4/12 = 1/3. Then both A and B (8 hours) run until full.
To find the time for a fraction, divide the fraction by the net rate. Filling half a tank at net rate 1/30 takes (1/2) ÷ (1/30) = 15 hours.

deepDiveAspects.title: Pipes with different diameters
deepDiveAspects.content: Sometimes the problem says pipe A is twice as fast as B. Then the rates are in the ratio 2 : 1. Use the ratio to find the individual times.

deepDiveAspects.title: Negative net rate
deepDiveAspects.content: If the outlet is faster than the inlet, the net rate is negative and the tank empties; the "time to fill" is meaningless. The time to empty is 1 ÷ |net|.

solvedExamples.title: Inlet and outlet
solvedExamples.question: A pipe can fill a tank in 10 hours and an outlet can empty it in 15 hours. If both are opened together, in how many hours will the tank be full?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The outlet slows down the filling.

solvedExamples.title: Leak
solvedExamples.question: A tap fills a tank in 6 hours. Because of a leak it takes 7.5 hours. In how many hours would the leak alone empty the full tank?
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Leak rate = tap rate − net rate.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The leak removes what the tap adds beyond the net.

solvedExamples.title: Three pipes
solvedExamples.question: Two pipes can fill a tank in 6 hours and 8 hours, and an outlet can empty it in 12 hours. If all three are opened together, how long to fill the tank?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The net rate is 5/24 of the tank per hour.

shortcutMethods.title: LCM litres

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Take the LCM of the times as the capacity, compute litres per hour for each pipe, add and subtract, divide.

rulesForApplication: Leak rate = tap rate − net rate.
Check that the time with a leak is longer.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Using time differences for the leak.
Assuming all pipes open at once.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: With an outlet, the combined fill time must be longer than the inlet alone.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Use the LCM method to avoid fractions.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Same logic as men and women in time and work.

intermediate.explanation: Capacity 24: +4, +3, −2 per hour. Net 5. Time = 24 ÷ 5 = 4.8 hours.

advanced.question: An inlet fills a tank in 8 hours and an outlet empties it in 12 hours. If the tank is half full and both are opened, the time to fill it is
advanced.explanation: Net = 1/8 − 1/12 = 1/24. The remaining half takes (1/2) ÷ (1/24) = 12 hours.

advanced.question: A tank has two inlets that fill it in 20 and 30 hours and a leak that empties it in 60 hours. With the leak, both inlets together fill it in

placementStyle.question: Pipes A and B fill a tank in 15 and 20 hours. Both are opened, but B is closed after 6 hours. The tank is filled in a total of
placementStyle.explanation: In 6 hours both fill 6 × (1/15 + 1/20) = 6 × 7/60 = 7/10. The remaining 3/10 by A alone takes (3/10) × 15 = 4.5 hours. Total 10.5 hours.

Pipe A fills a tank in 12 hours and pipe B empties it in 18 hours. Both are open for 6 hours, then B is closed. The time A then needs to fill the remaining tank is
placementStyle.explanation: In 6 hours the net is 6 × (1/12 − 1/18) = 6 × 1/36 = 1/6. Remaining 5/6 by A alone takes (5/6) × 12 = 10 hours.
